summary.text:
A short, clean outturn from a Surrey district that ends 2025/26 with no external long-term debt at all — the paper says so explicitly at page 6 ("As at 31 March 2026 the Council held no external long-term loans"). Reconciliation is trivial and it ties: our PWLB file returns "no borrower matching 'Reigate'" against the paper's zero. The only external borrowing is £13.0m of short-term LA-to-LA money at 4.57% weighted with WAM 102 days (Table 3 p.6), up £8.0m from £5.0m a year earlier as internal borrowing capacity thins.

The distinctive fact is not what Reigate's book looks like today but where it is heading and why. The liability benchmark (Table 8 p.10) rises from £5.2m at 31 March 2026 to £20.4m at 31 March 2027 and £26.1m at 31 March 2028 — a five-fold increase over two years, driven by CFR rising £15.8m and balance-sheet resources shrinking £5.1m. And LGR vesting to the new East Surrey Unitary lands at April 2027 — inside that window. The paper acknowledges the point openly at p.6: the debt-free approach "is likely to evolve" as capital investment needs rise and reserve-funded internal borrowing runs down.

A cross-council view worth naming: our PWLB file at 31 March 2026 shows the other three East Surrey districts that vest into the same unitary hold 30 PWLB loans totalling £215.94m at a weighted ~2.61% between them — Mole Valley 4 loans / £57.35m at 2.44%; Tandridge 21 loans / £94.17m at 2.77%; Epsom & Ewell 5 loans / £64.43m at 2.52%. Reigate is the only one of the four with no PWLB position. So the new unitary starts life with a substantial cheap long-dated PWLB book from three of its four constituent districts, and whatever Reigate does about long-term borrowing in the next twelve months becomes the fourth line on that opening balance.

Two other things worth flagging. On peer performance the paper's Table 5 shows Reigate returned 4.60% at 31/03/26 against 4.29% for "Similar Local Authorities" and 4.18% "All Local Authorities" (Arlingclose universe) — 31bp better than peers with 38% bail-in exposure against 58% peer, i.e. more return with less bail-in risk, largely because the £12m LA-to-LA loan at 5.20% (Table 4 p.7) sits alongside their MMFs and unsecured bank cash. And Reigate is on both sides of the inter-authority market at year end — borrowing £13m at 4.57% and lending £12m at 5.20%, a 63bp positive spread on the lend leg. The one soft spot is the commercial-income line (Annex 5.1 Section 5): net income drops from £1,161k to £247k because Redhill Distribution Centre is vacant; officers report marketing viewings underway in the covering report.

Andrew Barnett (Deputy CFO) and David Brown (Finance Manager) also named as authors, both with reigate-banstead.gov.uk addresses. Paper heard at O&S 11 June 2026 and Executive 25 June 2026. Council is being abolished April 2027 (East Surrey Unitary vesting), so window to correspond is limited.

officer.subject: Your zero-PWLB position, and the £216m the other three East Surrey districts hold
officer.body:
Hi Lisa,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature-repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are some thoughts on the Treasury Management Outturn 2025/26 that went to Overview and Scrutiny on 11 June and to the Executive on 25 June. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your paper is unusually clean for an outturn — the balance sheet identity ties across all four forecast years and the liability benchmark walk is one of the tidier presentations we've seen — and this is offered in that spirit.

The reconciliation is the shortest we've done. Your paper says at page 6 that the Council held no external long-term loans at 31 March 2026, and our PWLB file agrees — there is no borrower entry for Reigate and Banstead at all. Your £13.0m of external borrowing is LA-to-LA short-term at a weighted 4.57% with 102 days average maturity (Table 3). Which is the point of the reconciliation on this one: nothing ties to nothing, and both sides are recording the same fact.

The distinctive thing in the paper is not today's book but where it is heading. Your liability benchmark in Table 8 rises from £5.2m at 31 March 2026 to £20.4m at 31 March 2027 and £26.1m at 31 March 2028 — a five-fold increase over two years, driven by CFR rising £15.8m while balance-sheet resources fall £5.1m over the same window. Your page 6 flags it openly: "in the context of Local Government Reorganisation and the transition to the East Surrey Unitary authority from April 2027, this approach is likely to evolve." It is one of the more candid framings we have read of a debt-free position that is about to stop being debt-free — most reports in that spot avoid the sentence.

One thing we can see that a single-council paper cannot. Our PWLB file at 31 March 2026 shows the three other East Surrey districts vesting into the same unitary hold 30 PWLB loans totalling £215.94m at roughly 2.61% weighted between them — Mole Valley 4 loans at £57.35m weighted 2.44%; Tandridge 21 loans at £94.17m weighted 2.77%; Epsom and Ewell 5 loans at £64.43m weighted 2.52%. All maturity-profile, mostly 25 years and over. That is meant only as a data point, not a comment on any of those three papers — we have not read them. Reigate is the only one of the four with no PWLB position, so whatever the current Council decides about long-term borrowing in the next twelve months lands as the fourth line on the opening balance the new unitary inherits. Given the £20.4m need your own Table 8 flags for 31 March 2027, that decision is a live one this cycle.

One clean thing to name from your own numbers. Your investment benchmarking Table 5 shows a 4.60% return at 31 March 2026 against 4.29% for Similar Local Authorities and 4.18% for All Local Authorities in the Arlingclose universe. That is 31 basis points ahead of the peer group, and you got there with a bail-in exposure of 38% against 58% for the peer average — more return with less at-risk exposure, which is not the usual direction of that trade. The £12m LA-to-LA loan at 5.20% (Table 4) is doing most of the work. Worth also noting that you were on both sides of the inter-authority market at year end — borrowing at 4.57% and lending at 5.20% — a 63bp positive spread on the lend leg. Very few of the outturns we have read this year show that shape.

And a data point on rates rather than advice. Your Table on page 13 prints the PWLB certainty curve moving 22 to 45 basis points higher over the year even as Bank Rate fell 4.50% to 3.75% — 1y from 4.82% to 5.04%, 10y from 5.38% to 5.72%, 50y from 5.63% to 6.08%. Since 31 March the long end has continued to firm and the SONIA/OIS curve now prices Bank Rate above 4% at the one-year point, so if the £20.4m 2026/27 requirement gets met through PWLB fixed money the 5-10y band is where the read matters most. The full curve and every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO discount curve is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity and pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. Everything indicative and only the DMO can quote, and we model no MRP or accounting treatment on top.

Three courses fit. Liability Benchmark: the essentials is worth watching given your own benchmark is where the strategy conversation now sits, and CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates put it in front of everyone. Reading the PWLB certainty curve covers the mechanics of what has moved since your outturn was cut. And Short-term borrowing and the LA market speaks directly to how your 4.57% book compares with the £216m of long-dated PWLB the other three districts hold. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others — including your counterparts across the East Surrey workstream — would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell

officer.voice: Russell Tew, first-person. Deliberately not templated: no bold headers, no bulleted summary, contractions throughout.
